title: Anthropic's new hardware standard lets AI agents control the physical world
content:
For all the interest in and uptake of agentic AI systems over the past year or so, the world of automated AI has thus far been primarily limited to text, images, code, and other data and actions that take place inside a computer. Anthropic is now aiming to change that somewhat with what it’s calling the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a set of standardized drivers designed to let AI agents easily interface with and control arbitrary devices.
For now, the “research preview” of the MHS effort is being sold mainly as a way to help scientists streamline the arduous process of creating the custom software integrations that are often needed to get disparate components of an experiment working in concert. MHS can provide a common interface and common format for data sharing between these devices, Anthropic says, allowing them to talk to each other across a network “without needing a bespoke ‘translator’ program in between.” The standardized system could reduce weeks or months of exacting experimental setup down to “hours or minutes,” Anthropic writes.
In a video posted alongside the announcement, Anthropic Technical Staffer Alek Kemeny says the MHS effort was inspired by observing neuroscientist Arco Bast work through an experiment on memory formation in the brain at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. Kemeny said Bast had worked out an interface to get the rotating laser beams, microscopes, cameras, and myriad other components of the experiment to coordinate through a common interface. “This idea could be used to have AI run any science experiment in the world,” Kemeny recalls thinking at the time.
Your new robotic lab assistant?
There’s nothing about a common machine interface language that requires the use of AI models, of course. And Anthropic says MHS devices can be controlled directly in real time via command-line prompts and API code files. But integrating an MHS system with an AI model through the Model Context Protocol lets scientists interact with devices using natural language, and lets models “reason through each step in an experiment, update parameters in real time, and, in some cases, recover from hardware errors without intervention,” Anthropic writes.

report.summary: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard standardizes device drivers so AI agents can control lab hardware, reducing complex experimental setup from weeks to minutes.
report.background: Agentic AI has largely been confined to digital actions—text, images, code, and data within computers. Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard (MHS) aims to change that by providing standardized drivers that let AI agents interface with and control arbitrary physical devices. The research preview is initially positioned for scientific laboratories, where researchers often spend weeks or months writing custom software to make different instruments work together. MHS offers a common interface and data format, allowing lasers, microscopes, cameras, and other components to communicate across a network without bespoke translator programs. The effort was inspired by a neuroscientist's experiment on memory formation at HHMI Janelia Research Campus, where a custom interface coordinated many devices. Anthropic realized this approach could let AI run experiments worldwide. MHS can be used directly via command-line prompts and APIs, or integrated with AI through the Model Context Protocol for natural-language control.
key_points: MHS is a set of standardized drivers for hardware devices, letting different lab instruments share data through a common interface instead of requiring custom translators. This can cut experiment setup time from weeks or months down to hours or minutes, according to Anthropic.

The research preview focuses on scientific laboratories, where researchers often struggle to connect lasers, microscopes, cameras, and other equipment. Anthropic says a common format lets these components coordinate across a network without bespoke software, making complex experiments much easier to assemble.

MHS itself does not require AI. Users can control devices through command-line prompts and API code files. But when paired with Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, scientists can use natural language, allowing models to reason through steps, update parameters in real time, and sometimes recover from hardware errors automatically.

The idea came from observing a neuroscientist's memory-formation experiment at HHMI Janelia, where custom integration had been built. Anthropic realized the same approach could let AI run any science experiment in the world, expanding agentic AI from digital tasks to physical laboratory work.

Anthropic positions MHS as a research preview, suggesting the standard is still evolving. Its success will depend on whether device manufacturers adopt the interface and whether developers build tools around it. Broader applications beyond labs, such as robotics or industrial automation, may follow if the standard gains traction.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MHS marks a step toward giving agents physical-world agency, moving beyond screen-based tasks into real hardware control. Developers benefit from a standardized interface that could reduce custom integration work, especially when combined with Model Context Protocol for natural-language control. For regular users, the near-term impact is indirect: faster scientific discovery and more automated lab workflows. If the standard expands beyond research settings, it could eventually enable consumer robotics and smart-device automation. However, physical-world control raises serious concerns about safety, error handling, and accountability, so adoption will likely remain conservative outside controlled environments.
report.tools: Watch Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP), which pairs with MHS for natural-language control of devices. The MHS research preview itself offers command-line and API interfaces for developers. Open-source robotics and lab automation projects like Robot Operating System (ROS), EPICS, and PyLabLib provide alternative approaches to hardware abstraction and may inform or complement MHS implementations.
